passages.happening:
“After the plague had ended, the LORD said to Moses and Eleazar son of Aaron the priest, ‘Take a census of the whole congregation of Israel by the houses of their fathers—all those twenty years of age or older who can serve in the army of Israel’” (verses 1-2).

The count is taken ‘on the plains of Moab by the Jordan, across from Jericho’ (verse 3). It goes tribe by tribe, and within each tribe clan by clan. Simeon now has 22,200 men (verse 14). Judah has 76,500 (verse 22).

The list pauses at a few names. Under Reuben it recalls Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed with Korah: “They serve as a warning sign. However, the line of Korah did not die out” (verses 10-11). Under Manasseh it notes a man with no sons: “The names of his daughters were Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah” (verse 33).

“These men of Israel numbered 601,730 in all” (verse 51).
passages.hearers:
The book began with a count at Sinai. That count listed the generation that came out of Egypt. Nearly forty years have passed. The sentence spoken at Kadesh has run its course, and the last plague is over. Now God orders a second count. With it the book turns from the old generation to the new.

Almost everything is the same as in chapter 1: the same age, the same purpose, the same twelve tribes. Two things are different. Aaron is dead, and his son Eleazar stands beside Moses. And the place has changed. The first count was taken in the desert of Sinai. This one is taken within sight of the land.

The total is the most striking thing. At Sinai there were 603,550. Now there are 601,730. A whole generation has died in the desert, and the people is almost exactly the size it was. God had said that the parents would fall and the children would be brought in. The second list is the proof that he kept the children alive.

Set side by side, the two lists show changes inside the total. Simeon has fallen from 59,300 to 22,200. Many interpreters connect that with Peor, where the leader who sinned so publicly was a Simeonite (25:14). Manasseh has grown from 32,200 to 52,700.

This chapter gives more than chapter 1 did. It names the clans within each tribe, most of them called after the sons and grandsons of Jacob listed in Genesis 46. The word for clan is the commonest word in the chapter. That is because this count has a second purpose. It is a list of heirs. Land in Israel was held by families and handed down, and to be named in a clan was to have a share in the land ahead.

The places where the list pauses are worth noticing. One recalls the rebels of chapter 16 as ‘a warning sign’, and at once adds that Korah's family survived. One names five sisters, which a list of fighting men had no need to do. Their story is the next chapter.
passages.later:
Genesis lists the sons and grandsons of Jacob who went down to Egypt, seventy persons in all (Genesis 46:8-27). Their names have become the clans of a nation.

God had promised Abraham offspring beyond counting (Genesis 15:5). Moses said to this generation, “The LORD your God has multiplied you, so that today you are as numerous as the stars in the sky” (Deuteronomy 1:10).
passages.hard:
Can the numbers be right, with more than 600,000 fighting men?

The same question arose in chapter 1. A force of that size would mean two million people or more, and that is hard to fit with what is known of the Sinai desert and of the population of Canaan at the time.

Christians and Jews who hold Scripture in high regard have answered in several ways. Some take the numbers as they stand and point to God's provision in the wilderness, which the text itself stresses. Some note that the Hebrew word elef, usually ‘thousand’, can also mean a clan or a military unit, so that a figure like 43,730 might once have meant forty-three units with 730 men. This reading has to explain why the totals in the text add up as thousands. Some take the figures as symbolic, a way of saying that God's promise to multiply Abraham's family had been kept. Others think they reflect a later count.

No answer has won general agreement, and these notes take no side. The notes on 1:20-46 and on Exodus 12:37 set out the question. What the chapter cares about is the comparison. A generation died, and God raised up another of nearly the same size.
passages.asks: After forty years of funerals, the people numbered almost exactly what they had at the start. Ask where you have assumed that a long season of loss has left God's purposes smaller. And ask what the generation after you is being made ready for, and what part you have in that.

passages.t: How the land will be shared
passages.happening:
God tells Moses how the land is to be divided. “The land is to be divided among the tribes as an inheritance, according to the number of names” (verse 53). A large tribe is to receive more and a small tribe less (verse 54).

“Indeed, the land must be divided by lot” (verse 55).
passages.hearers:
This short passage shows what the count was for. The first census prepared an army. This one also prepares a settlement. For the first time in the book a list of names looks forward to fields and towns.

Two principles are joined. The size of each share follows the size of the tribe. That is plain fairness: more people need more land. But where each tribe's land will lie is settled by lot.

The lot was a way of deciding by casting marked objects. In Israel it was not thought of as chance. It was a way of putting a decision into God's hands. Its use here meant that no tribe could say that Moses or Joshua had favored another. The powerful could not choose the best land for themselves. The LORD assigned the territories.

The key word is ‘inheritance’. In Hebrew it is nachalah, the same word God used in chapter 18 when he told the Levites that he himself was their share. An inheritance is not earned or bought. It is received because of the family a person belongs to. Israel will not hold the land as a prize of war. It will hold it as a gift from its Father. That word will govern the rest of the book.
passages.later:
Proverbs gives the conviction behind the lot: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33).

The book of Joshua tells how the lots were cast at Shiloh, ‘in the presence of the LORD’ (Joshua 18:10).

The New Testament takes up the word for all who belong to Christ: “And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise” (Galatians 3:29). Peter writes of ‘an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading’ (1 Peter 1:4).
passages.asks: The land was shared by need and placed by lot, so that no one could seize the best for himself. Ask how you would feel if your place in life had been assigned in a way that left no room to push ahead of others. And ask what you hold that you treat as earned, when it was given.

passages.t: The Levites, and two men left
passages.happening:
The Levites are counted separately, by their three clans. The list traces one family in particular: Amram and his wife Jochebed, and their children ‘Aaron, Moses, and their sister Miriam’ (verse 59). It recalls that two of Aaron's sons, Nadab and Abihu, ‘died when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD’ (verse 61). The Levites number 23,000. They are counted apart ‘because no inheritance was given to them among the Israelites’ (verse 62).

Then the chapter closes. “Among all these, however, there was not one who had been numbered by Moses and Aaron the priest when they counted the Israelites in the Wilderness of Sinai. For the LORD had told them that they would surely die in the wilderness. Not one was left except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun” (verses 64-65).
passages.hearers:
The Levites are listed last and apart, as in the first census. They will receive no territory, so they are not counted among the heirs. Chapter 18 gave the reason: God himself is their share.

The family of Moses is named here in full, with his mother Jochebed. By now Aaron and Miriam are dead. The list is a memorial as much as a record.

Then come the two sentences on which the whole book turns. God had said at Kadesh that the men counted in the first census would die in the wilderness, all but two. Here the writer checks the two lists against each other and reports the result. Not one name from Sinai is on the list from Moab, except Caleb and Joshua.

It is said without comment. No one gloats, and no lesson is drawn. The word God spoke in chapter 14 has simply been kept, both parts of it. The generation that refused the land is gone. And the children they feared for are standing, counted and named, at the edge of the land.

Caleb and Joshua walked the whole forty years with a generation whose unbelief they had not shared. They are now old men among the young. They are also the living link between the promise made at Sinai and those who will receive it.
passages.later:
Caleb later spoke of these years himself: “Now behold, as the LORD promised, He has kept me alive these forty-five years since He spoke this word to Moses, while Israel wandered in the wilderness” (Joshua 14:10).

Hebrews draws its warning from the generation that fell: “So we see that it was because of their unbelief that they were unable to enter” (Hebrews 3:19). The warning is written to Christians about themselves. The same letter adds a promise: “There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9).
passages.asks: Caleb and Joshua kept faith for forty years among people who had not, and lived to see the promise. Ask where you are being asked to stay faithful over a long time, with little company. And ask which of God's words to you has two parts, a warning and a promise, and whether you believe both.
